questions.q: Why is lie detection so hard, according to the summary?
a: Communication is complex and our biases distort our judgment
Most people lie less often than scientists expect
Body language is the only reliable source of clues
Trained professionals are the only ones who can spot lies
questions.why: Lesson 1 points to the difficulty of tracking verbal and nonverbal cues at once, plus the power of bias.

questions.q: What is a “convincing statement” in the summary?
a: A claim about one’s own honesty meant to reinforce your trust
A direct yes or no answer to a direct question
A detailed account of events with exact times
An admission made after a long silence
questions.why: Lesson 2 says liars use lines like “it’s not in my nature” to shore up your faith in them.

questions.q: Why might a liar repeat your question back to you?
a: To buy time to think of an answer
To show that they were listening closely
To correct a mistake in how you phrased it
To signal that they are about to confess
questions.why: Lesson 2 explains that repeating a question stalls for time and fills an awkward silence.

questions.q: When do suspicious cues become meaningful?
a: When several of them appear together in a cluster
When a single cue appears exactly once
When the person avoids eye contact for a moment
When the interview lasts more than an hour
questions.why: Lesson 2 stresses that individual cues mean little; clusters of verbal and visual cues suggest deception.

questions.q: Why should you avoid asking the same question over and over?
a: It lets the person rehearse the lie until it sounds convincing
It makes the interview take far too long
It gives the person time to calm down
It is considered rude in professional settings
questions.why: Lesson 3 warns that repetition helps a liar practice and strengthens their story.
